card.questionRef: 2015 HL Q9(a) — roof/wall junction at eaves
card.stem: Design the external envelope of the two-storey house to be thermal bridge free. It has a 450 mm concrete-block external wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity, a traditional cut roof, tongue-and-groove first-floor boards on timber joists, and an insulated solid-concrete ground floor. The original diagram circles FOUR junctions: roof/wall at eaves; upper floor/external wall; window cill; ground floor/external wall. Part (a) selects any THREE of these four. A window head appears in the scheme commentary but is NOT a fifth circled option.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show best-practice detailing that prevents a thermal bridge at the roof/wall junction at eaves. This is one 16-mark location from the printed choose-three task.

rows.contextNote: Continue the wall and roof insulation through the eaves junction rather than leaving a conductive gap. The source model includes 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation, a 60 mm cavity closer, AAC block, 60 mm rigid insulation board and 400 mm fibreglass insulation. Coordinate the eaves construction and required ventilation; do not bridge the insulation with a continuous conductive element. Award the published 8-mark notes allowance for this one selected location; the scheme prints no finer breakdown.

Draw and label a coherent section through the roof/wall junction at eaves, showing how the insulation remains continuous. Use the corresponding model illustration with the original house specification. This is the separate published 8-mark sketch allowance, not another notes allowance.

card.questionText: Discuss the importance of designing a building envelope that is thermal bridge free.

rows.verbatim: Discussion (point 1) - 2 marks for point, 4 marks for discussion
rows.contextNote: Give a distinct valid point (2) and develop its importance (4). Source-supported routes include reduced heat loss and heating demand; more even internal surface temperatures and comfort; less risk of cold surfaces reaching dew point, condensation and mould; less material deterioration and associated health effects. Explain the causal relationship, not just a label, and avoid repeating the other point. Thermal bridging is local increased conduction; airtightness alone does not remove every conductive bridge.

card.stem: Design the external envelope of the two-storey house to be thermal bridge free. It has a 450 mm concrete-block external wall with a 250 mm full-fill insulated cavity, a traditional cut roof, tongue-and-groove first-floor boards on timber joists, and an insulated solid-concrete ground floor. The original diagram circles FOUR junctions: roof/wall at eaves; upper floor/external wall; window cill; ground floor/external wall. Part (a) selects any THREE of these four. A window head appears in the scheme commentary but is NOT a fifth circled option.
card.questionText:
Using notes and freehand sketches, show best-practice detailing that prevents a thermal bridge at the roof/wall junction at eaves. This is one 16-mark location from the printed choose-three task.

Using notes and freehand sketches, show best-practice detailing that prevents a thermal bridge at the upper-floor/external-wall junction. This is one 16-mark location from the printed choose-three task.

Using notes and freehand sketches, show best-practice detailing that prevents a thermal bridge at the ground-floor/external-wall junction. This is one 16-mark location from the printed choose-three task.

Discuss the importance of designing a building envelope that is thermal bridge free.

rows.contextNote: Continue the wall and roof insulation through the eaves junction rather than leaving a conductive gap. The source model includes 250 mm full-fill cavity insulation, a 60 mm cavity closer, AAC block, 60 mm rigid insulation board and 400 mm fibreglass insulation. Coordinate the eaves construction and required ventilation; do not bridge the insulation with a continuous conductive element. Award the published 8-mark notes allowance for this one selected location; the scheme prints no finer breakdown.

Draw and label a coherent section through the roof/wall junction at eaves, showing how the insulation remains continuous. Use the corresponding model illustration with the original house specification. This is the separate published 8-mark sketch allowance, not another notes allowance.

Keep the insulation continuous past the timber first floor and prevent joists from penetrating the inner leaf into the insulated cavity. The scheme shows joists on metal hangers with resin-anchored support at the inner leaf and plastered wall surfaces. Maintain the specified tongue-and-groove boards on joists and show the uninterrupted insulated cavity. Award the published 8-mark notes allowance for this one selected location; the scheme prints no finer breakdown.

Draw and label a coherent section through the upper-floor/external-wall junction, showing how the insulation remains continuous. Use the corresponding model illustration with the original house specification. This is the separate published 8-mark sketch allowance, not another notes allowance.

Continue wall insulation down past the floor edge and connect it with the ground-floor insulation. The source examples include an 80 mm perimeter insulation strip up to finished floor level, wall insulation at least 225 mm below the finished floor, 150–300 mm floor insulation and AAC blocks at the inner leaf below ground. Show the insulated solid-concrete ground floor and avoid a conductive slab-to-wall bypass. Award the published 8-mark notes allowance for this one selected location; the scheme prints no finer breakdown.

Draw and label a coherent section through the ground-floor/external-wall junction, showing how the insulation remains continuous. Use the corresponding model illustration with the original house specification. This is the separate published 8-mark sketch allowance, not another notes allowance.

rows.verbatim: Discussion (point 1) - 2 marks for point, 4 marks for discussion
rows.contextNote: Give a distinct valid point (2) and develop its importance (4). Source-supported routes include reduced heat loss and heating demand; more even internal surface temperatures and comfort; less risk of cold surfaces reaching dew point, condensation and mould; less material deterioration and associated health effects. Explain the causal relationship, not just a label, and avoid repeating the other point. Thermal bridging is local increased conduction; airtightness alone does not remove every conductive bridge.
